title: Test as the account the app actually runs under
explanation: `sudo -u billing cat /etc/billing/billing.conf` fails with `Permission denied`. Testing with plain `sudo cat` instead would succeed and hide the problem entirely -- root reads anything regardless of file permissions, and the app never runs as root.

title: Confirm what's actually blocking it
explanation: `ls -l /etc/billing/billing.conf` shows `-rw------- root root` -- mode `600`. Only the owning UID (`root`) has any access at all; `billing` falls into "other" and gets nothing. That fully explains the failure -- no ACL, no capability, just a plain mode that never accounted for the app's own account.

title: Grant access to exactly the account that needs it, not to everyone
explanation: The file holds a secret (`db_password`, `api_key`), so the fix isn't `chmod 644` -- that would make it world-readable to every account on the box. Either `sudo chown billing /etc/billing/billing.conf` (keeps it at `600`, now owned by the app's own user) or `sudo chgrp billing ... && sudo chmod 640 ...` (readable by the `billing` group only) grants the minimum needed.

title: Verify as the app's own user again
explanation: `sudo -u billing cat /etc/billing/billing.conf` should now print the config contents. Checking with `sudo cat` here would be meaningless -- it was never in question that root could read it.
